To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HCL is caused by the interaction of two constraints, one phonetic and one phonemic, and that PCS is a consequence of a higher-ranked phonemic constraint.

HCL is the result of the phonetic constraint that vowels and sonors are longer before voiced obstruents and that PCS is a result of a conjoined constraint that prohibits long vowels and sonors before voiceless obstruents.

(i) the difference between H CL and PCS is the result of the difference of the combination of the preceding consonant clusters, and (ii) HCL and PCS can be unified under one constraint hierarchy, and (iii) HCL and other vowel changes are not incompatible.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to account for the phonetic and phonological factors that are relevant for HCL and PCS, and to what extent the two changes can be treated as a single phenomenon.
the question of how HCL and PCS can be integrated into the overall picture of the quantitative changes in ME.

how the phonetic tendency of lengthening before voiced obstruents interacts with phonemic length and with other quantitative changes, and how the constraints on HCL are ranked with those on other changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HCL is the consequence of the interaction of the phonetic constraint and the phonemic one, and that HCL is not incompatible with PCS, but rather a part of the same process.
HCL was a phonetic tendency that was not always realized as a phonological change.
HCL and PCS are not incompatible with each other, but rather are complementary.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the quantitative change of vowels in ME is the result of a complex interaction of phonological, phonetic, and orthographic factors.
HCL is not exceptional, and that the quantitative changes of ME vowels are not as chaotic as previously thought.

a more accurate analysis of ME vowels is possible when the interaction of different constraints is considered. The main takeaway from our work is that
the quantitative changes of English vowels can be accounted for by a unified set of ranked constraints.
the quantitative change in the history of English is not a random process but is rather a systematic one, which is constrained by a number of factors.

the quantitative changes in vowels are not independent of one another, but rather interdependent, and that the phonetic tendency of the lengthening of vowels and sonorant before a voiced obstruents is a key to the explanation of these changes in vowels.
